etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle French revenge, a derivation from revenger, from Old French revengier (possibly influenced by Old Occitan revènge (“revenge, comeback”), from Old Occitan revenir (“to come back”)), a variant of Middle French revancher, from Old French revenchier. The variants Old French vengier (whence French venger) and Old French venchier are both descended from Latin vindicō, with stress-conditioned different parallel development in the inflectional forms. Compare avenge and vengeance.

definitions.definition: Any form of personal, retaliatory action against an individual, institution, or group for some alleged or perceived harm or injustice.
A win by a previous loser.

quote.citation: 1908, W[illiam] B[lair] M[orton] Ferguson, chapter I, in Zollenstein, New York, N.Y.: D. Appleton & Company, →OCLC:
quote.text: “I'm through with all pawn-games,” I laughed. “Come, let us have a game of lansquenet. Either I will take a farewell fall out of you or you will have your sevenfold revenge”.

quote.citation: 1999 January 27, Bride of Chaotica! (Star Trek: Voyager) (Science Fiction), Paramount Domestic Television, →OCLC:
quote.text: CHAOTICA: Arachnia, death as you know it has no hold on me. My defeat is but a temporary setback. I shall return to seek my revenge.JANEWAY: He doesn't give up, does he?PARIS: They never do. CHAOTICA: Our love was not meant to be, my Queen. But be warned. You have not seen the last of (gurgle) Chaotica.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English revengen, from Old French revengier, revenger.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To take revenge for (a particular harmful action) or on behalf of (its victim); to avenge.

quote.citation: 1697, Virgil, “The First Book of the Æneis”, in John Dryden, transl., The Works of Virgil: Containing His Pastorals, Georgics, and Æneis. […], London:  […]  Jacob Tonson, […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The gods are just, and will revenge our cause.

quote.citation: 1814, Lord Berners, The Ancient Chronicles of Sir John Froissart:
quote.text: to revenge the death of our fathers

quote.citation: c. 1840, Leigh Hunt, The Seer; Or, Common-places Refreshed:
quote.text: However, my veneration for that illustrious man was so great, that on the night when he died, I revenged him finely on his two principal enemies.

definitions.definition: (transitive, reflexive) To take one's revenge (on or upon someone).

quote.citation: 1599 (first performance), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Iulius Cæsar”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act IV, scene iii]:
quote.text: Come, Antony, and young Octavius, come,  Revenge yourselves alone on Cassius.

definitions.definition: (intransitive, archaic) To take vengeance; to revenge itself.

quote.citation: c. 1591–1592 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Third Part of Henry the Sixt, […]”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iv]:
quote.text: a bird that will revenge upon you all

quote.citation: 1814, Dante Alighieri, “Canto VII”, in H[enry] F[rancis] Cary, transl., The Vision; or, Hell, Purgatory, and Paradise, of Dante Alighieri. […], volume III (Paradise), London:  […]  [J. Barfield] for Taylor and Hessey, […], →OCLC, page 30, lines 45–47:
quote.text: Count it not hard henceforth, when thou dost hear  That a just vengeance was by righteous court  Justly reveng'd.  […]
